paras: The killing of Charlie Jackson was the fatal shooting of a Black man, named in reports as Charlie, Charles or Charley Jackson, by a constable's party of officers and citizens in Gonzales County, Texas, in February 1888, after he was accused of shooting the county's sheriff, Albert Little. Texas reports said Constable J. C. Nugent shot Jackson through the breast after Jackson fired at him, while a widely reprinted wire brief said Little had been killed and that a posse "riddled" Jackson with bullets. The first report from Luling also forecast that "Judge Lynch" would deal with Jackson that night, but no later report described a lynching.

Albert Little was identified in most reports as the sheriff of Gonzales County, though the Brenham Weekly Banner called him a "Deputy Sheriff." According to a special from Luling dated February 7, Little had tried the night before to arrest Jackson on the farm of a Mr. Eckais, spelled "Eckols" in the Austin Weekly Statesman, in Gonzales County. None of the reports said what Jackson was wanted for.

In the Luling special's account, Jackson was hidden in a house on a dark night and fired at Little three times without being seen, leaving the sheriff thought fatally wounded, with his recovery "considered doubtful." The next morning Constable Nugent of Luling set out with a party of Gonzales County officers and citizens to search for Jackson. When Nugent came upon him, the special said, Jackson fired once, and as he was about to fire again Nugent shot him through the breast, a wound the dispatch called fatal. The Brenham Weekly Banner, which gave Jackson the alias "Hicks," likewise reported that he was "shot fatally" by Nugent the day after Little was shot.

A shorter dispatch datelined Luling, February 8, told the story differently, saying Little "was killed last night by a negro desperado named Jackson" and that a posse overtook Jackson "and riddled him with bullets."

The Luling special noted that Little had "many friends" where the shooting took place and said it was thought "Judge Lynch" would attend to Jackson's case that night, a forecast printed under a headline that described Jackson as "Himself Wounded." No report of a lynching, an inquest into Jackson's death, or Little's death, funeral or recovery appears in the coverage.

In Texas the Luling special ran at length: the Fort Worth Daily Gazette ran it on February 8 as "Probable Double Killing," with the deck "A Negro shoots an Officer While Resisting Arrest, and is Himself Wounded," and the Austin Weekly Statesman ran it on February 9 under "An Officer Shot and Mortally Wounded by a Negro in Ambush." The Statesman's version omitted the closing line about "Judge Lynch," and the Brenham Weekly Banner later condensed the story to a single item among its state news on February 16.

Outside Texas, the short wire version ran on February 9 in the St. Paul Daily Globe under "A Sheriff Killed," in the Richmond Dispatch, and in the Georgia Morning News under the heading "A Murderer Bullet-Riddled." Over the next three weeks the item was rewritten as a one-sentence paragraph in news-digest columns in papers from Indianapolis and Great Bend, Kansas, to Atlanta and Lake Charles, Louisiana, with "last night" becoming "the other night" or "recently." These copies identified Jackson only by his surname as "a negro" or "a negro desperado" and stated the sheriff's death as fact; the Lake Charles Echo dated it "the 8th inst.," and the last copy found appeared on February 29.

Accounts differed on whether Little died: the Luling special called him fatally wounded with doubtful recovery, the wire brief said he was killed, and the Brenham Weekly Banner said only that he was shot. They also differed on the date, since the special dated February 7 placed Little's shooting on the previous night, while the wire dispatch of February 8 said "last night" and the Indianapolis Journal's copy said "Tuesday night." The special attributed the fatal shot to Nugent alone after an exchange of fire, while the wire said the posse riddled Jackson; both versions came from the pursuers' side, and the special was the earlier and more detailed local report.

reader.title: Killing of Charlie Jackson
bases: Jackson was shot dead by a constable leading a party of county officers and citizens searching for him after he was accused of shooting the sheriff (A1, A2, A11); the wire credits 'a posse' (A4).

Jackson was killed by a pursuing party of officers and citizens led by Constable Nugent, who by the Luling special's account shot him after Jackson fired first, while making an arrest search rather than an extralegal punishment (A1, A2, A11); the wire's 'riddled him with bullets' (A4) and the special's forecast that 'Judge Lynch' would act (A1) come from reports that describe no seizure or execution by a mob.

The Luling special (A1, A2) and the separately worded Luling wire brief (A4, A3) agree that Jackson shot Sheriff Little and was then killed by the pursuing party, and the Brenham Banner (A11) agrees, though they differ on details.

accounts.gist: Jackson, hidden in a house, fired three times at Sheriff Little, wounding him probably fatally; next morning Constable Nugent's party found him, Jackson fired once, and Nugent shot him through the breast as he was about to fire again.

accounts.label: Brenham Banner state news
accounts.gist: Deputy Sheriff Little was shot Tuesday night near Luling by Charley Jackson, alias Hicks, whom he was trying to arrest; the next day Constable Nugent shot Jackson fatally.

framing.detail: The Fort Worth Gazette headed it 'Probable Double Killing' with 'A Negro shoots an Officer While Resisting Arrest,' and closed by forecasting that 'Judge Lynch' would attend to the case, without comment.
The Austin Statesman headlined 'An Officer Shot and Mortally Wounded by a Negro in Ambush' and dropped the lynching forecast.
The wire brief called Jackson a 'negro desperado' and reported the posse riddling him as a fitting sequel; the Georgia Morning News headed it 'A Murderer Bullet-Riddled.'
Digest columns reprinted the one-sentence wire item through Feb. 29, with 'last night' softened to 'the other night' or 'recently.'
